list.listitem: Patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension but no variceal hemorrhage should undergo screening EGD B and treatment with beta-blocker if large varices are found. A
Endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) as prophylaxis should be reserved for patients who have contraindications or cannot tolerate beta-blockers. A
EGD performed within 12 hours should be used to make the diagnosis and treat variceal hemorrhage with EVL or sclerotherapy. A
EVL is the treatment of choice for patients with current or prior bleeding. A
Short-term (maximum 7 days) antibiotic prophylaxis should be instituted in any patient with cirrhosis and GI hemorrhage. A

background.definition: Esophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins that develop in patients with underlying portal hypertension. Gastroesophageal variceal hemorrhage is common and a major complication of portal hypertension resulting from cirrhosis. It accounts for 10% to 30% of all cases of bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract (UGI). See also topic on non-variceal UGI hemorrhage. and topic on esophageal varicies.

list.listitem: Cirrhosis affects 3.6 out of every 1000 adults in North America.
Variceal hemorrhage occurs in 25% to 40% of patients with cirrhosis.
The incidence of gastric varices is lower than esophageal varices ranging from 2-20%.
Ten to thirty percent of all variceal bleeds are caused by gastric varices. Gastric varices are associated with higher risk of rebleeding, higher rate of transfusion, and higher mortality .
Variceal hemorrhage is associated with higher morbidity and mortality than other causes of gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB) as well as with higher hospital costs.
The complications associated with portal hypertension substantially contribute to 32,000 deaths and greater than 20 million days of work loss associated with cirrhosis annually in the United States.
Esophagogastric varices develop as a consequence of systemic or segmental portal hypertension (PH).
Chronic liver disease leading to cirrhosis is the most common cause of portal hypertension (increased portal venous pressure). Likelihood can be predicted using a clinical decision rule.
The most common causes of systemic portal hypertension in the US are alcoholic liver disease and chronic active hepatitis.

Esophageal varices form as a result of increased portal pressure. Portal venous pressure is directly related to blood flow and resistance through the liver as described by Ohm's law: P = Q x R, where P is the pressure along the vessel, Q is the flow, and R is the resistance to flow.

Portal hypertension in cirrhosis results from increased intrahepatic resistance (at the presinusoidal, sinusoidal, and postsinusoidal locations) as well as increased flow through hyperdynamic splanchnic system.
Imbalance between the potent vasoconstrictor endothelin-1 and the potent vasodilator nitric oxide has been suggested as an important factor in the genesis of increased resistance.

Portal hypertension results in the development of collateral circulation, including venous channels in the esophagus and stomach, by the dilation of preexisting vessels and active angiogenesis. Esophagogastric varices increase in size with the severity of portal hypertension and can rupture when the tension in their walls exceeds a maximal point.

The normal hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) is 5 mm Hg or less; anything above this value denotes portal hypertension. Varices may develop but generally do not bleed if the HVPG is less than 12 mm Hg.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Location of varices in EG junction
Appearances of the varices: red wale marks and cherry red spots

list.listitem: Patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension but no variceal hemorrhage should undergo screening EGD B and treatment with beta-blocker if large varices are found. A
Reserve endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) for patients who have contraindications for or cannot tolerate beta-blockers. A
Patients with small varices at screening EGD should have a repeat EGD in 1 to 2 years and those with no varices in 3 years. C
Following variceal eradication, repeat EGD every 6 to 12 months and treat recurrent varices with EVL. C
Patients with cirrhosis who present with upper GI bleeding (from varices or other causes) should be given prophylactic antibiotics, preferably before endoscopy. A

Patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension but no prior variceal hemorrhage (especially those with platelet counts <140,000/mm3 or Child's Class B or C) should undergo screening EGD and treatment with beta-blocker if large varices are found.
Patients with cholestatic liver disease may have relatively preserved liver function and platelet counts so screening may be recommended sooner.

The optimal surveillance intervals for esophageal varices have not been determined. For patients found to have no varices on initial screening endoscopy, repeat endoscopy at 3 years intervals has been suggested, whereas patients with small varices should undergo endoscopy in 1 to 2 years.
Esophageal varices may grow faster in patients with alcoholic cirrhosis, severe liver impairment, or endoscopic stigmata of high risk ("red wale markings"). These patients should undergo yearly EGD.

A small study investigating liver stiffness measurement (LSM) and spleen diameter as predictors for esophageal varices in 123 patient's with chronic hepatitis C. The authors determined that the overall accuracy of these measurements approached 98% for detecting varices in this patient population.

Because of the high mortality rate associated with the initial variceal hemorrhage, primary prevention is indicated. Non selective beta-blockers (eg, propranolol or nadolol), given in doses to reduce the pulse rate by 25%, have been shown to prevent or delay the first episode of variceal bleeding (NNT = 2.8) for prevention of first variceal bleeding.
Early beta-blocker therapy may slow the rate of growth of small esophageal varices.
Endoscopic variceal ligation is effective for primary prophylaxis, but in most cases, it is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate or who have contraindications to beta-blocker therapy.
N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA) injection for primary prevention of fundal varices could improve survival.

In a recent metaanalysis including 604 patients with gastric varices, the endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided-injection and/or coiling of varices was highly successful in obliterating varices either in the primary or the secondary prevention. In primary prevention, the efficacy was 90.2%, and with combined coil and glue was 95.4%, and the rebleeding risk was 4.9%. In the secondary prevention, the total efficacy was, with glue was 84.6%, with coil was 92.3%, with combined coil/glue was 84.5%, while the risk of rebleeding was 18.1%, and the risk of recurrence was 20.6%.
Beta-blockers decrease the rate of variceal rebleeding (NNT = 5.5) and increases survival (NNT = 14.3) in patients with cirrhosis and esophageal varices surviving an initial episode of GI bleeding.

Among 12,009 patients with acute GI bleeding (45% with suspected variceal bleeding) tranexamic acid (an antifibrinolytic agent) given as a 1 gram loading dose with a 3 gram maintenance dose over 24 hours, was not superior to placebo for death from r-ebleeding but was associated with a higher risk of venous thromboembolic events and seizures.

The optimal approach to the prevention of recurrent variceal hemorrhage in patients with cirrhosis is uncertain. A decision analysis suggested that combination therapy with medications and band ligation was the optimal strategy, with transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunts (TIPS) reserved for those with poor compliance.

A study randomized 144 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma and esophageal varices to propranolol or endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL). The EVL group had significantly fewer episodes of bleeding and lower mortality (30 vs 40 deaths).

The goal of long-term treatment is prevention of rebleeding, hepatic decompensation, and death. Orthotopic liver transplantation is the only treatment that reliably achieves all 3 objectives. Cirrhotic patients with Child class B or C should be listed for transplantation unless a contraindication exists.
Prophylactic antibiotics in cirrhotic patients hospitalized for bleeding lead to overall reduction in infectious complications and possibly decreased mortality (RR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.55-0.95).

However, in cirrhosis with acute upper GI bleeding, shorter-duration or no antibiotic prophylaxis appears noninferior to standard duration therapy of 5 to 7 days for mortality, though evidence quality is low. However, shorter or no prophylaxis may increase early rebleeding and bacterial infections, so routine prophylaxis remains reasonable until higher-quality data clarify this tradeoff.
Antibiotics may also reduce the risk of recurrent bleeding in hospitalized patients who bled from esophageal varices.

However a 2025 meta-analysis suggests that shorter durations of antibiotic prophylaxis (or even no prophylaxis) are non-inferior to the standard 5–7 day course for preventing mortality in patients with cirrhosis and acute upper GI bleeding. But shortening or omitting antibiotics was associated with a higher incidence of bacterial infections and early rebleeding. Given the low quality of evidence, current guidelines recommending 5–7 days of prophylaxis remain the standard of care until better data emerges.
Balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) when used in secondary prevention of gastric varices could improve survival.

In a recent Cochrane review, the secondary prevention of variceal bleeding using portosystemic shunts versus endoscopic intervention with and without medical treatment was examined. The authors concluded that there was very low certainty whether the interventions reduced all-cause mortality (RR 0.99; 95%CI: 0.86-1.13), rebleeding caused mortality (RR 0.4; 95%CI: 0.33-0.5), rebleeding (RR 0.51; 95% CI 0.34-0.76), and acute (RR 1.6; 95% CI: 1.33-1.92) or chronic (RR 2.51; 95% CI: 1.38-4.55) hepatic encephalopathy occurrence. There was no data on the effect of the interventions on the quality of life.

In a case report on 3 patients with gastric varices, n-butyl-cyanoacrylate (nBCA)-assisted retrograde transvenous obliteration (NARTO) through the gastrorenal shunt under balloon occlusion was simpler procedure to the original or modified balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration and more cost effective but needs further validation.
In a retropsective study on 60 patients (70% with IGV1, and 30% with GOV2), it was found that histoacryl injection is safe with a risk of rebleeding only of 8.3%.

Foam scelrotherapy (using sodium tetradecyl sulfate [STS] foam) with ballon anetgrade blocking of the varix was applied on 12 patients with esophageal, gastric, rectal, jeujenal or duodenal varices and was found highly effacious and safe.

A systematic review identified 24 observational studies, mostly case series, and found rates of hemostasis of gastric varices using endoscopic injection of cyanoacrylate of 65% to 100%, but a pooled recurrence rate of 34%.
Suspect variceal bleeding in a patient with known or suspected hepatic cirrhosis who presents with GI bleeding. C
EGD is the diagnosis test of choice for esophageal varices. A

Establishing the correct diagnosis is important. Other causes of upper GI bleeding more common in patients with liver disease include Mallory Weiss tear, portal hypertension, and gastric antral vascular ectasia. A

Differential.Differential_Features: History of alcohol binge or NSAID use or previous history of peptic ulcer disease
Typically, history of repeated retching or vomiting
History of cirrhosis of the liver
Typically patients are >70 years old, female, with iron deficiency anemia, and with no history of cirrhosis
History of weight loss, smoking, and alcohol consumption

list.listitem: Esophageal gastric varices commonly present with acute onset of hematemesis, with or without hemodynamic compromise. Variceal bleeding usually is severe, resulting in hypovolemia manifested by postural vital signs or shock.
There may be preceding retching or dyspepsia attributable to alcoholic gastritis or withdrawal. Varices per se do not cause symptoms of dyspepsia, dysphagia or retching.
Important elements of the history include history of alcohol consumption, chronic liver disease, or variceal bleed.

CBC, platelet count, coagulation studies, serum creatinine, and liver enzymes should be obtained early in evaluation of a patient with UGIB. Cross-matching for 2 to 4 units or more of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) should be done very early. Because the hematocrit may take 24 to 72 hours to equilibrate with extravascular fluid, it is not a reliable indicator of severity of acute bleeding.

Upper panendoscopy is the diagnostic modality of choice for acute upper GI bleeding (UGIB). Endoscopy is highly sensitive and specific for locating and identifying bleeding lesions in the upper GI tract. Endoscopy in patients with UGIB is also effective in treating most causes of UGIB and is associated with a reduction in blood transfusion requirement and length of intensive care unit and total hospital stay.
If portal venous system thrombosis is suspected, endoscopic ultrasound may be helpful in confirming the diagnosis.
The combination of nasogastric aspiration and lavage has a relatively low sensitivity and negative predictive value for upper GI bleeding, and is therefore inadequate to rule out an upper GI source.
The sensitivity of CT angiography in detecting active acute UGI bleeding is 85.2%, and it is 92.1% specific in localizing the site of bleeding.
The Rockall clinical decision rule can be used to estimate inpatient mortality risk after acute upper GI hemorrhage.
The Glasgow-Blatchford score (GBS), compared to the pre-endoscopic and complete Rockall score, performs better in predicting high-risk patients presenting with UGI bleeding.

A clinical decision rule has been developed that noninvasively estimates the probability of the presence of varices in patients with established cirrhosis. It is based on the ratio of platelet count to the maximal spleen diameter.

The C-WATCH Score was developed to predict the composite of recurrent bleeding, need for intervention, or 30 day mortality among patients with an acute UGI bleed, before endoscopy. Mean age was 64 years, 33% female.

Classification of fundal gastric varices : The three most commonly used classifications of fundal varices are: Sarin’s, Hashizome, and Arakawa’s classifications. Sarin’s classification includes: Gastroesophageal varix (GOV) type 1: it is a small extension from the esophagus on the lesser curvature of the stomach; Gastroesophageal varix type 2: the extension is on the greater curvature; Isolated gastric varix (IGV) that has no relation to the esophagus either in stomach (type 1) or duodenum (type 2).
AASLD includes in the most important classifications also: Saad-Caldwell, Kiyosue, Hirota and Matsumoto Classifications.

There are three types of gastric varices according to endoscopic classification: Cardiofundal gastric varices which are located posteriorly and/or at the greater curvature of the stomach, they have a separate blood supply from the esophageal varices. While lesser curvature gastric varices are located on the lesser curvature with the same blood supply as esophageal varices. In addition to distal gastric varices, a rare type of gastric varices mostly assciated with splenic vein thrombosis. Therapy for active gastric varcies could be guided by this classification, along with other clinical and radiological data of the patient. However, AGA (American Gastroenterological Association) does not recommend primary prophylaxis based on the endoscopic classification.
The older classification (Sarin classification) is not helpful in deciding the proper treatment plan.
Assessment of hemodynamic stability and resuscitation if necessary should be done before any diagnostic study.
Validated clinical decision rules can predict in patient mortality in patients with GI bleed, such as the Glasgow-Blatchford score.
Endoscopy is the diagnostic modality of choice for esophagogastric varices.
If endoscopy is inconclusive and gastric varices are suspected, endoscopic ultra-sound may be useful in differentiating gastric varices from gastric fold.
See algorithm in .
Provide hemodynamic resuscitation and transfuse as needed to a hemoglobin of approximately 8 g/dL. C
In patients with current or prior bleeding from esophageal varices, endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) is the preferred treatment and superior to sclerotherapy. A
After an episode of bleeding, patients should undergo repeat EVL every 2 to 4 weeks until the varices are eradicated. C Concomitant beta-blocker use should be considered. A
Endoscopic sclerotherapy (EST) should be reserved for patients that fail EVL. C

Salvage treatment with TIPS or surgery is recommended when medical and endoscopic treatment fails; a recent RCT also found improved mortality and reduced rebleeding with early TIPS compared with usual therapy. B

Short-term antibiotics (maximum 7 days) should be started in any patient with cirrhosis and GI hemorrhage. Oral norfloxacin (400 mg twice daily) or IV ciprofloxacin is the recommended antibiotics. Patient with advanced cirrhosis should be given IV ceftriaxone (1 g/day).

Octreotide (a long-acting analog of somatostatin) will decrease portal venous inflow, portal pressures, azygos flow, and intravariceal pressures. Accepted dosing for octreotide in patients presenting with UGI bleed suspected to be variceal is a 50 mcg bolus followed by 50 mcg per hour. Optimal duration has not been established but many studies have used 5 days.

In patients with esophageal variceal hemorrhage post-band ligation, a 24-hour octreotide infusion was non-inferior to a 72-hour infusion for preventing rebleeding (0% vs. 11%, p = 0.49) with no significant differences in transfusion need, infection, or other complications.

In a Cochrane review of 21 small studies of somatostatin drugs or their analogs for patients with acute or recent variceal bleeding, there was no reduction in mortality. The risk of rebleeding was only significantly reduced in the lower quality trials and the need for blood transfusion was minimally reduced (one half unit per patient).

While octreotide is the drug of choice in the US due to availability, terlipressin is the drug of choice in countries where it is available since it is the only pharmacologic treatment associated with a demonstrated reduction in mortality compared with placebo.

A recent RCT compared vasoconstrictors (e.g. somatostatin or terlipressin) to proton pump inhibitors among 118 patients presenting with variceal bleeding who achieved immediate hemostasis with endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL). It concluded that there was no differences in clinical outcomes between the two groups in terms of immediate re-bleeding and overall treatment failure. However the rate of adverse events was much higher in the vasoconstrictor group (55%) vs. the PPI group (6%).

A meta-analysis of endoscopic therapy with or without beta-blockers found significant study heterogeneity but reported a possible decrease in overall and recurrent bleeding with combined therapy than either treatment alone; there was no mortality benefit.

In 2 small RCTs of EVL (also called band ligation) with or without combination beta-blocker/isosorbide mononitrate, there was no benefit of combined therapy over either therapy alone (rebleeding was between one quarter and one third of patients).

The human recombinant activated factor VII is one of the suggested treatments for UGIB in patients with liver disease. However, a Cochrane review found no evidence that it reduces the risk of death in these patients.
There is no evidence for or against the use of vitamin K in the treatment of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with liver disease.

Among 503 patients on dabigitran (Pradaxa) and experiencing uncontrollable or life-threatening bleeding or who required rapid reversal of the anticoagulant, idarucizumab (two 2.5-mg infusions of the study drug 5 minutes apart) reversed the anticoagulation effects of dabigatran in more than 98% for 24 hours.

According to the AGA guidelines, treatment of actively bleeding gastric varices is best injected by cyanoacrylate without lipidol. Repeating endoscopy in a 2-4 weeks period is mandatory to inject residual varices, then when the condition stabilizes follow up of the patient is recommended in 3-6 months period, then annually.
Hemostatic powder could act as a bridge therapy in acute bleeding, by mechanically blocking the bleeding.
A recent RCT published showed that hemostatic powder used in acute bleeding episode of esophageal varices could improve early and 6 weeks survival.

Endoscopic therapy is the definitive treatment of choice for active variceal hemorrhage. This should be performed within 12 hours. Endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) is the treatment of choice for controlling active bleeding and for secondary prophylaxis in obliterating varices. EVL is superior to endoscopic sclerotherapy (EST) in eradicating varices more rapidly with less recurrent bleeding and fewer complications.

Among 516 patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding with high risk features (Glasgow-Blatchford score of 14 with 10% having bleeding esophageal varices), early endoscopy (within 6 hours) was not superior to delayed endoscopy (within 24 hours) for 30 day all-cause mortality, further episodes of bleeding, duration of hospitalization or percentage of patients receiving transfusions.

In an RCT of EST versus emergency portacaval shunt (EPCS) in patients with actively bleeding varices and cirrhosis, EPCS was significantly more effective in permanently stopping bleeding (100% vs. 20% with EST) and improving survival. There were also fewer episodes of recurrent encephalopathy with EPCS versus EST (15% vs. 35%, respectively). EST may also offer no advantage over vasoactive medications listed above.

Balloon tamponade is an effective way to achieve short-term hemostasis. The main problem is the high risk of rebleeding following deflation of the balloon. In addition, there can be significant complications such as esophageal perforation. It should only be used as a temporary measure for up to 24 hours.
There are 2 types of surgery for control of variceal hemorrhage: shunt operations and non-shunt operations. Surgery should be considered by highly expert surgeons at tertiary centers.

Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunts function like side-to-side surgical portacaval shunts without general anesthesia or major surgery. This is done by expert interventional radiologists. TIPS should be considered in patients in whom hemorrhage from fundal varices cannot be controlled. An RCT of 63 patients did find less rebleeding (NNT = 2) and reduced mortality (NNT = 4) in patients receiving early TIPS (within 72 hours) versus standard therapy.
In patients who bleed from gastric fundal varices, endoscopic variceal obstruction using tissue adhesives such as cyanoacrylate is preferred, where available. EVL is also an option.

In several small case series, stent placement (allowing food and fluid to pass but providing compressive hemostasis over the bleeding varices) stopped the bleeding in 78% to 100% of patients, and no patients experienced re-bleeding within 60 days. However 15% to 32% of patients required follow-up procedures (e.g. band ligation, TIPPS insertion) after the removal of the stent. A 2011 NICE guideline concluded that stents are effacious in selected patients in whom other methods to control bleeding have failed.

In a recent Cochrane review, the secondary prevention of variceal bleeding using portosystemic shunts versus endoscopic intervention with and without medical treatment was examined. The authors concluded that there was very low certainty whether the interventions reduced all-cause mortality (RR 0.99; 95%CI: 0.86-1.13), rebleeding caused mortality (RR 0.4; 95%CI: 0.33-0.5), rebleeding (RR 0.51; 95% CI 0.34-0.76), and acute (RR 1.6; 95% CI: 1.33-1.92) or chronic (RR 2.51; 95% CI: 1.38-4.55) hepatic encephalopathy occurrence. There was no data on the effect of the interventions on the quality of life.

The general principles of management of a patient with UGI bleed suspected to be variceal are: hemodynamic resuscitation, prevention and treatment of complications, and treatment of bleeding. Hemoglobin of approximately 8 g/dL should be maintained.

Among 921 patients with severe acute UGI bleeding, a restrictive transfusion policy (transfuse when hemoglobin drops below 7 g/dl) was associated with better 6-week survival outcomes (95% vs. 91%) compare to a liberal transfusion policy (transfuse when hemoglobin drops below 9 g/dl). Additionally, the rate of re-bleeding was lower in the restrictive-strategy group (10% vs. 16%) as were adverse events (40% vs. 48%). Additionally, among patients with cirrhosis (Child-Pugh disease class A or B), survival was 30% higher in the restrictive vs. liberal transfusion groups.
A slightly higher transfusion of 8 g/dl is recommended for patients with myocardial ischemia.
Complications related to bleeding and to the treatment of bleeding contribute substantially to mortality.
Four principle complications that cause death are aspiration pneumonia, sepsis, hepatic encephalopathy, and renal failure.
Patients with cirrhosis presenting with GI bleed should receive prophylactic antibiotics.
In hospital mortality has improved with the use of vasoactive drugs, endoscopy, and antibiotic prophylaxis. A
The rate of all-cause inpatient mortality for upper GI hemorrhage was 1.9% in 2012.B
Mortality after the initial hemorrhage in patients with cirrhosis may be as high as 50% with a 30% mortality associated with subsequent bleeding episodes. C

There are two distinct phases in the course of variceal hemorrhage, an acute phase and a later phase in which there is a high risk of recurrent bleeding. The acute phase starts with the onset of active bleeding.
Mortality after the initial hemorrhage in patients with cirrhosis is up to 50%.
Only 50% of patients with variceal hemorrhage stop bleeding spontaneously. Patients with Child class C cirrhosis and large, active spurting varices are less likely to achieve spontaneous hemostasis.

Following cessation of active bleeding, there is a period of approximately 6 weeks in which there is a high risk of recurrent hemorrhage. The greatest risk is within the first 72 hours and over 50% occur within the first 10 days.
Approximately 70% of all untreated patients die within the first year after their initial variceal bleed.
The causes of death include recurrent variceal hemorrhage, liver failure, hepatic encephalopathy, and progressive ascites and infections.

A new bleeding risk score (A4C) for older adults (≥80) on DOACs may predict major bleeding better than existing scores, incorporating factors like age, anemia, renal function, albumin, and amiodarone use. However, it is derived from a single cohort and can still misclassify risk, so it should be used cautiously and not replace clinical judgment.
The rate of all-cause inpatient mortality for upper GI hemorrhage was 1.9% in 2012.
In-hospital mortality has improved threefold over the last 2 decades. This is likely due to increased use of vasoactive drugs, endoscopy, and antibiotics prophylaxis.
Active variceal hemorrhage accounts for one third of all deaths related to cirrhosis. One year survival for those who survive 2 weeks after a variceal bleed is approximately 52%.
The risk of bleeding and of death in patients who survive 6 weeks is similar to that of cirrhotic patients of equivalent severity who have never bleed.
Approximately 70% of all untreated patients die within the first year after their initial variceal bleed.
Validated clinical decision rules can predict in patient mortality in patients with GI bleed, such as the Glasgow-Blatchford score.

The optimal surveillance intervals for esophageal varices have not been determined. For patients found to have no varices on initial screening endoscopy, repeat endoscopy at 3 years intervals has been suggested, whereas patients with small varices should undergo endoscopy in 1 to 2 years.
Following an episode of bleeding from esophageal varices, EVL should be performed every 2 to 4 weeks until the varices are eradicated.
Alcohol should be stopped completely.
Patients may need to be evaluated at a liver transplant center if they are appropriate candidates.

Patients who are elderly or have cardiovascular disease are at a high risk of having acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and should be monitored appropriately. Consideration should be given to ruling out AMI.

listitem.strong: Using vasoconstrictive drugs with caution in elderly or patients with cardiovascular ischemia.

list.listitem: High-risk patients (the elderly or those with multiple comorbidities) should be transfused with packed red blood cells to keep their hematocrit above 30 g/dL.

cell.label: Variceal hemorrhage suspected (patient with known or suspected cirrhosis)?
See chapter on nonvariceal upper GI hemorrhage.
Perform initial clinical assessment, initial resuscitation and stabilization, and admit (usually to ICU).
Give IV octreotide or somatostatin and perform urgent/emergent endoscopy with endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) or endoscopic sclerotherapy (EST) if EVL not possible. Assess outcome.
Repeat esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) every 1-2 weeks until varices obliterated. Repeat EGD at 1-3 months, then every 6-12 months to check for recurrence.
Balloon tamponade, octreotide or somatostatin. Successful?
EVL (EST if EVL not possible). Bleeding stops?
